The complete blood count (CBC) is the foundational hematologic test in neonatal care. It includes hemoglobin (Hb), hematocrit (Hct), red blood cell indices (MCV, MCH, MCHC, RDW), white blood cell count with automated and manual differential, platelet count, and reticulocyte count.

When to obtain a neonatal CBC:

  • Risk factors for sepsis (maternal fever, PROM >18h, GBS positive/unknown)
  • Clinical signs: pallor, plethora, jaundice, petechiae, bleeding
  • Maternal history: diabetes, preeclampsia, TORCH, alloimmunization
  • Abnormal prenatal findings (hydrops, IUGR, TTTS)
  • Traumatic delivery (vacuum, forceps) — evaluate for hemorrhage
  • Temperature instability, poor feeding, lethargy, respiratory distress

Five-Step CBC Interpretation Framework:

  1. Hb/Hct normal for GA and postnatal age? Low → anemia pathway. High → polycythemia. Always use age-appropriate references.
  2. Reticulocyte count? High retic (>6–8%) = hemorrhage or hemolysis (marrow responding). Low retic (<2%) = hypoproliferative (marrow failing).
  3. Direct Coombs (DAT) positive? Positive = immune hemolysis (Rh, ABO, minor antigens). Negative = non-immune or hemorrhage.
  4. Platelet count? Low = thrombocytopenia pathway. Timing matters: early (<72h) vs late (>72h) determines differential.
  5. Coagulopathy? Prolonged PT/aPTT = assess for DIC, VKDB, liver disease, or inherited factor deficiency.
⚠️ Critical Pitfall: Capillary (heel-stick) Hct overestimates venous Hct by 5–15%. ALWAYS confirm with a venous sample before making treatment decisions.

1. CBC with reticulocyte count and peripheral smear — severity and morphology
  2. Direct Coombs test (DAT) — positive = immune hemolysis
  3. Blood type and Rh — maternal AND infant
  4. Total and direct bilirubin — indirect ↑ supports hemolysis
  5. Kleihauer-Betke on MATERNAL blood — if hemorrhage suspected
  6. Based on DAT result:
    DAT+ → antibody ID panel
    DAT− + high retic → G6PD screen, EMA test, Hb electrophoresis
    DAT− + low retic → parvovirus B19 PCR, bone marrow if persistent
⚠️ Anti-Kell pitfall: Suppresses erythropoiesis AND causes hemolysis. Retic may be LOW despite immune hemolysis. Don't be reassured by low bilirubin in anti-Kell disease — anemia can be severe.

Protocol: 10–20 mL/kg pRBC (Hct ~60%) over 2–4 hr. Irradiated, leukoreduced, CMV-safe, O Rh-compatible. Assigned-unit system to limit donor exposures.

Prevention:

  • DCC 30–60 sec → 27% fewer transfusions (Cochrane 2019)
  • Minimize phlebotomy — micro-sampling, POC testing
  • Iron 2–4 mg/kg/day starting 2–4 weeks in preterm
  • EPO: modest benefit, no NDI benefit (PENUT, NEJM 2020); NOT recommended routinely
✓ Continue enteral feeds during RBC transfusion. Transfusion-associated NEC not consistently demonstrated (TOP subanalysis 2022).

Hemorrhagic anemia = blood loss, acute or chronic. DAT negative, normal smear morphology, initially normal bilirubin (acute). Reticulocyte count elevated.

  • Acute: pallor, tachycardia, hypotension, poor perfusion, normal bili
  • Chronic: compensated, hepatosplenomegaly (extramedullary hematopoiesis), elevated retics
  • Bilirubin initially NORMAL (no RBC destruction releasing bilirubin)
  • MCV may be elevated from reticulocytosis (reticulocytes are large cells)

1. ABCs: Airway/breathing secured. IV access ×2.
  2. Volume: NS 10–20 mL/kg bolus. Repeat for HR >180, CRT >3s, hypotension.
  3. Emergency blood: Uncrossmatched O-neg pRBCs 10–15 mL/kg.
  4. Crossmatched pRBC: 10–20 mL/kg over 2–4 hr (faster if shock).
  5. Coagulopathy: Vitamin K 1 mg IV. FFP 10–15 mL/kg. Cryo 5–10 mL/kg if fib <100.
  6. Identify source: KB test, cranial US, abdominal US, serial HC.
  7. Monitor: Serial Hb q4–6h. HC q30min if subgaleal. Strict I&O.
  8. Transfer Level III/IV if ongoing hemorrhage or hemodynamic instability.

🚨 Subgaleal hemorrhage is LIFE-THREATENING. The space can hold the entire blood volume (~80 mL/kg = 240–320 mL in a term neonate).

Subgaleal Hemorrhage Protocol:

  1. Recognize: Boggy, fluctuant swelling that CROSSES suture lines. Often shifts with gravity.
  2. Measure HC immediately and every 30 minutes. Increase >1 cm = concerning.
  3. Establish IV ×2. STAT CBC, T&S, PT/aPTT/fibrinogen.
  4. Volume resuscitation: NS 10–20 mL/kg. Repeat PRN.
  5. pRBC 10–15 mL/kg. Use O-neg uncrossmatched if emergent.
  6. Correct coagulopathy: Vit K 1 mg IV. FFP 10–15 mL/kg. Cryo if fib <100.
  7. Pressure wrap (ACE around head) — may slow hemorrhage.
  8. Transfer Level III/IV NICU immediately.

IVH Papile Classification:

GradeDescriptionPrognosis
IGerminal matrix hemorrhage onlyExcellent; resolves
IIIVH without dilation (<50%)Generally favorable
IIIIVH WITH dilation (>50%)Risk hydrocephalus/NDI
IV*PVHI (periventricular hemorrhagic infarction)High risk CP/NDI

*Grade IV now termed PVHI — venous infarction, not IVH extension.

Fetomaternal Hemorrhage (FMH): Fetal blood crosses placenta into maternal circulation. Small FMH (<1 mL) in 50–75% of pregnancies (insignificant). Large FMH (>30 mL) = severe neonatal anemia or hydrops.

  • Acute: pallor, shock, normal bilirubin
  • Chronic: compensated anemia, high retics, hepatosplenomegaly, possible hydrops
  • RhoGAM dose adjustment needed for Rh-neg mothers if large FMH (>30 mL = additional vials)

TTTS: Unbalanced flow through vascular anastomoses in monochorionic placentas.

  • Donor twin: anemic (Hb often <8), growth-restricted
  • Recipient twin: polycythemic (Hct often >65%), may develop hydrops from volume overload

TAPS (Twin Anemia-Polycythemia Sequence): Chronic slow TTTS causing large inter-twin Hb difference (>8 g/dL) WITHOUT amniotic fluid discordance.

Kleihauer-Betke Test:

  • Performed on MATERNAL blood (not infant)
  • Acid elution: adult Hb eluted by acid; HbF resists → fetal cells visible as dark "ghost cells"
  • % fetal cells × maternal blood volume (~5,000 mL) = FMH volume
  • Detects FMH >5 mL; may miss smaller hemorrhages
  • False positives: maternal sickle trait, hereditary persistence of fetal Hb
  • Flow cytometry: more accurate alternative using anti-HbF antibodies
⚠️ When to send KB test: Any unexplained neonatal anemia with elevated retics, normal bilirubin, and negative DAT. Order on the MOTHER, not the infant.

IVH Screening Protocol:

  • Cranial US for ALL infants <32 weeks at 7–14 days of life
  • Repeat at 36–40 weeks PMA (evaluate for PVL)
  • Earlier US if acute neurologic deterioration

IVH Prevention Strategies:

  • Antenatal steroids (most effective single intervention)
  • Delayed cord clamping 30–60 sec
  • Gentle handling in first 72 hours
  • Head midline positioning
  • Avoid wide blood pressure swings
  • Correct coagulopathy promptly
  • Avoid rapid volume expansion

Hemolytic anemia = premature RBC destruction. Hallmarks: anemia with elevated retic, indirect hyperbilirubinemia, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin (unreliable in neonates).

The DAT (Coombs test) is the critical branch point: positive = immune; negative = non-immune.

FeatureImmune (DAT+)Non-Immune (DAT−)
MechanismMaternal IgG crosses placenta, destroys fetal RBCsIntrinsic RBC defect (membrane, enzyme, Hb)
DATPositiveNegative
Common causesRh (anti-D), ABO, Kell, c, EG6PD, HS, PK def, α-thalassemia
SmearSpherocytes (ABO), nRBCs (Rh)Spherocytes (HS), bite cells (G6PD), targets (thal)
SeverityRh: can be severe/hydrops. ABO: usually mildG6PD: episodic severe. HS: variable. α-thal major: lethal

DAT-Positive Workup:

  1. Antibody identification — anti-D, anti-A/B, anti-Kell, anti-c, anti-E
  2. Maternal + infant blood type/Rh
  3. Serial TSB — plot on 2022 AAP nomogram. Rise >0.5 mg/dL/hr = accelerated hemolysis
  4. Reticulocyte count — elevated in ABO/Rh; may be LOW in anti-Kell (erythropoiesis suppression)
  5. CBC — anemia severity, nucleated RBC count

Management:

  • Phototherapy per 2022 AAP guidelines
  • IVIG 0.5–1 g/kg — may reduce exchange transfusion need in Rh disease
  • Exchange transfusion — double volume (160–180 mL/kg), removes ~85% circulating bilirubin
  • pRBC transfusion for significant anemia
🚨 Anti-Kell: Suppresses erythropoiesis + causes hemolysis. Retic may be LOW. Anemia more severe than bilirubin suggests. Absence of jaundice does NOT exclude severe anemia.

DAT-Negative Workup Algorithm:

  1. Peripheral smear: Spherocytes → HS or ABO; Bite cells/Heinz bodies → G6PD; Target cells → hemoglobinopathy; Schistocytes → DIC/microangiopathy
  2. G6PD quantitative assay — screen all unexplained DAT-neg jaundice. PITFALL: levels falsely NORMAL during hemolysis (reticulocytes have more G6PD). Repeat in 2–3 months.
  3. EMA binding test — decreased = hereditary spherocytosis. More reliable than osmotic fragility in neonates.
  4. Hb electrophoresis — HbF predominates in neonates. α-thal major shows Hb Bart's (γ4 tetramers).
  5. PK assay — if smear/other tests non-diagnostic; 2nd most common RBC enzymopathy.
⚠️ G6PD is the #1 risk factor for kernicterus worldwide. Now on the RUSP for newborn screening in many US states. Jaundice can be rapid and severe.

Rh HDFN:

  • Rh-neg mother sensitized to D antigen → anti-D IgG crosses placenta → destroys Rh-pos fetal RBCs
  • Spectrum: mild jaundice → severe anemia + jaundice → hydrops fetalis
  • Prevention: RhoGAM 300 µg IM at 28 wk + within 72h of delivery. Reduced incidence >95%.
  • DAT strongly positive (3–4+). Smear: nucleated RBCs, polychromasia

ABO Incompatibility:

  • Mother O, baby A or B. Natural anti-A/B are IgG in group O mothers
  • Can occur in FIRST pregnancy (no prior sensitization needed)
  • Usually MILDER than Rh. DAT may be weakly positive or even negative
  • Rarely causes hydrops; primarily jaundice requiring phototherapy
  • Smear: spherocytes (mimic HS; context + DAT distinguish them)

AntibodyFrequencySeveritySpecial Notes
Anti-Kell3rd most commonCan be SEVERESuppresses erythropoiesis → low retic is a PITFALL
Anti-cIncreasingly recognizedModerate–severeCan cause hydrops
Anti-ECommonUsually mildRarely needs exchange
Anti-DuffyUncommonMild–moderateDuffy-neg common in Black individuals

Exchange Transfusion Protocol:

  • Indication: TSB at/above exchange threshold on 2022 AAP nomogram, OR rising >0.5/hr despite intensive phototherapy + IVIG
  • Volume: Double blood volume = 160–180 mL/kg
  • Blood: O Rh-neg, irradiated, CMV-safe, crossmatched against maternal + infant serum, Hct 40–50%
  • Access: UVC with tip in IVC (preferred). Alternative: UVC + UAC isovolumetric
  • Technique: Push-pull 5–10 mL/kg aliquots alternating
  • Monitoring: Continuous cardiac. Glucose/Ca/K/bili after every 50–100 mL. CaGluconate 10% 1 mL per 100 mL blood exchanged (citrate chelates Ca)
  • Removes: ~85% bilirubin, ~70% antibody-coated RBCs
🚨 Complications: Hypocalcemia, hyperkalemia, thrombocytopenia, infection, NEC, PVT, arrhythmia, air embolism. Mortality ~0.3–1%. Only at experienced centers.

G6PD Deficiency:

  • X-linked recessive; ~400 million affected worldwide. Males of African, Mediterranean, Asian descent.
  • G6PD maintains glutathione → protects RBCs from oxidative damage
  • Neonatal presentation: severe jaundice days 2–5, often disproportionate to anemia
  • Triggers: infection, naphthalene (mothballs), sulfonamides, primaquine, fava beans
  • Smear: bite cells, blister cells, Heinz bodies (require supravital stain)
  • Diagnosis: G6PD quantitative assay. Levels falsely normal during hemolysis — repeat 2–3 months later

Hereditary Spherocytosis (HS):

  • AD in ~75% (ankyrin, spectrin, band 3). 25% de novo/AR.
  • Membrane cytoskeleton defects → spherical RBCs → splenic trapping/destruction
  • Neonatal: jaundice, anemia (may need transfusion), splenomegaly (may be absent)
  • Diagnosis: Spherocytes + elevated MCHC >36 g/dL (most sensitive parameter). EMA binding test = preferred in neonates.
  • Family history positive in 75% — check parents' CBC and smear
  • Splenectomy reserved for severe disease, deferred until >5–6 years

α-Thal major (Hb Bart's)ARAll 4 α genes deleted → hydrops, usually lethalHb electrophoresis (Hb Bart's = γ4)
α-Thal HbH (3 gene)ARMild-mod microcytic anemia, neonatal hemolysis possibleHb electrophoresis
Hereditary elliptocytosisADUsually mild; neonatal poikilocytosisSmear: elliptocytes

Hypoproliferative anemia = reticulocyte count LOW or inappropriately normal for degree of anemia — bone marrow not responding. Most commonly = anemia of prematurity. Rare: DBA, Fanconi, parvovirus, TAM.

ConditionFrequencyKey FeaturesDiagnosis
Anemia of prematurityVery commonEPO suppression + short RBC lifespan + growth + phlebotomyClinical context; low retics in preterm at 4–8 wk
DBA~7/millionPure red cell aplasia, macrocytic, elevated HbF/eADA, anomalies 50%Elevated eADA; RPS19 most common gene
Parvovirus B19Rare neonatalTransient aplastic crisis; absent retics; hydrops if in uteroIgM/PCR
Fanconi anemia~1/160,000Progressive pancytopenia + anomalies (thumbs, café-au-lait, short stature)Chromosome breakage (DEB/MMC)
TAM~10% of T21Circulating blasts, hepatosplenomegaly, GATA1 mutationSmear + flow cytometry

Anemia of Prematurity — Management:

  • Pathophysiology: (1) EPO suppression, (2) short RBC lifespan (60–70d vs 90–120d), (3) rapid growth dilution, (4) iatrogenic phlebotomy (VLBW lose 10–20% blood volume/week)
  • Nadir: 7–9 g/dL at 4–8 weeks
  • Prevention: DCC (27% reduction), minimize draws, iron 2–4 mg/kg/day
  • Transfusion: Per 2024 restrictive thresholds

DCC 30–60 sec+1.2 g/dL Hb, 27% fewer transfusions✅ Strongly recommended
UCMMay = DCC; concern IVH <28 wk⚠️ Not recommended <28 wk
Minimize phlebotomyVLBW lose 10–20% BV/week✅ Micro-sampling, POC
EPOModest; no NDI benefit (PENUT)❌ Not routinely recommended
Iron supplementationSupports erythropoiesis✅ 2–4 mg/kg/day at 2–4 wk

Suspect rare congenital cause when:

  • Low retics in a TERM infant (AOP is a preterm diagnosis)
  • Macrocytic anemia (MCV >110 fL) without obvious cause
  • Physical anomalies + anemia = DBA or Fanconi
  • Pancytopenia = bone marrow failure syndrome
  • Circulating blasts + trisomy 21 = TAM
  • Anemia not responding to iron/EPO after weeks
🔬 Refer to hematology for: unexplained term anemia, anomalies + anemia, persistent anemia, circulating blasts, pancytopenia.

Respiratory support = any invasive/non-invasive ventilation, CPAP, HFNC, or O₂ >21%.

• Volume: 10–20 mL/kg (15 mL/kg most common)
  • Rate: Over 2–4 hours via pump
  • Product: pRBCs Hct ~60%, irradiated, leukoreduced, CMV-safe
  • Type: Group O, Rh-compatible. Assigned-unit system (single donor for multiple transfusions)
  • Expected rise: ~3 g/dL per 15 mL/kg
  • Post-transfusion: Recheck Hb 4–6 hours
  • Feeds: Continue at pre-transfusion rates
See Anemia of Prematurity tab in parent node for complete prevention strategies including DCC, phlebotomy minimization, iron supplementation, and EPO evidence.

• Pure red cell aplasia; presents typically 2–6 months
  • Macrocytic anemia, elevated HbF, elevated eADA, low retics
  • Anomalies in 50%: triphalangeal/absent thumbs, cardiac (VSD/ASD), craniofacial (Pierre Robin)
  • ~70% have ribosomal protein gene mutations (RPS19 = 25%)
  • Treatment: corticosteroids (70% respond), chronic transfusions, HSCT for severe
  • Elevated cancer risk: MDS, AML, osteosarcoma

• Inherited bone marrow failure; progressive pancytopenia (may not manifest until age 5–10)
  • Neonatal clues: absent/hypoplastic thumbs (40%), café-au-lait spots (40%), short stature, renal anomalies (30%), cardiac (15%)
  • Diagnosis: chromosome breakage test (DEB/MMC)
  • >20 FANC genes (AR except FANCB = X-linked)
  • Treatment: androgens, HSCT (only cure), cancer surveillance

• Tropism for erythroid precursors; halts red cell production
  • Fetus: severe anemia → hydrops → fetal death (greatest risk 13–20 wk)
  • Neonate: transient aplastic crisis with retic near 0%, resolves 1–2 weeks
  • Diagnosis: B19 IgM (may be neg in neonates); PCR more reliable
  • Treatment: supportive; pRBC transfusion. In utero: intrauterine transfusion.

• ~10% of trisomy 21 neonates. Circulating megakaryoblasts, leukocytosis (WBC can be >100K), hepatosplenomegaly
  • GATA1 mutations on chromosome X
  • Self-resolving in 80% within 1–3 months
  • BUT 20–30% develop AMKL within 1–4 years
  • Diagnosis: smear (blasts), flow cytometry (CD41+/CD61+), GATA1 testing
  • Low-dose cytarabine for severe cases (hepatic failure, DIC)
🔬 Any T21 neonate with blasts: hematology consult. Even if TAM resolves, serial CBC q3 months for 4 years to detect AMKL.

Neonatal polycythemia: venous Hct > 65% or Hb > 22 g/dL. Prevalence 1–5% of term neonates. Venous Hct peaks at 6–12 hours. Viscosity increases exponentially above Hct 65%.

⚠️ NEVER diagnose or treat based on capillary Hct. Overestimates by 5–15%. Always confirm with VENOUS sample.

Active (↑ erythropoiesis)Chronic fetal hypoxia → ↑ EPOIUGR/SGA, maternal DM, smoking, high altitude, T21/T18/T13, Beckwith-Wiedemann, CAH
Passive (RBC transfusion)Extra RBC volume transferredProlonged DCC (>3 min), TTTS recipient, maternal-fetal transfusion, cord milking (if excessive)

SystemSymptomsIncidence

1. Confirm VENOUS Hct
  2. Assess symptoms (CNS, GI, metabolic, respiratory)
  3. Check glucose and calcium
  4. Decision:
    • Hct 65–70% + asymptomatic → ↑ PO fluids 10–20%; recheck 12–24h; glucose q2–4h
    • Hct 65–70% + symptomatic → PET
    • Hct ≥ 70% regardless → PET

PET Protocol:

  • Formula: Vol = BV × (Obs Hct − 55) / Obs Hct. BV = 80–100 mL/kg.
  • Example: 3.5 kg, Hct 72%: (85×3.5) × (72−55)/72 = 70 mL
  • Fluid: Normal saline (preferred over albumin/plasma)
  • Access: UVC push-pull in 5 mL/kg aliquots
  • Post-PET: Recheck Hct 4–6h. Glucose q2h for 12–24h.
ℹ️ PET improves short-term symptoms but has NOT improved long-term neurodevelopmental outcomes (Cochrane review, Dempsey & Barrington).

• Increase oral fluids 10–20%
  • Monitor glucose q2–4h (hypoglycemia in 12–40%)
  • Recheck venous Hct in 12–24h
  • Assess for new symptoms each nursing assessment
  • If symptoms develop or Hct rises ≥70% → proceed to PET

• Venous Hct ≥ 70% regardless of symptoms
  • Venous Hct 65–70% WITH significant symptoms (seizures, respiratory distress, severe feeding intolerance, cyanosis)
  • Refractory hypoglycemia in setting of polycythemia

1. Confirm venous Hct. Calculate: Vol = BV × (Obs Hct − 55) / Obs Hct
  2. Obtain informed consent (risks: NEC, infection, thrombosis)
  3. Place UVC — confirm tip on X-ray (IVC above diaphragm)
  4. Pre-PET labs: CBC, glucose, Ca, bili
  5. Withdraw 5 mL/kg over 2–3 min → infuse equal NS → repeat until total volume exchanged
  6. Monitor: HR, RR, BP, SpO₂ continuously during procedure
  7. Post-PET: Hct (target 50–55%), glucose, Ca at 1h and 4–6h

• NEC (lower risk with NS vs colloid replacement)
  • Infection (procedural)
  • Thrombocytopenia (dilutional, usually mild/transient)
  • Air embolism, vessel perforation, thrombosis (UVC-related)
  • Rebound polycythemia (recheck 4–6h and 24h)
ℹ️ NS is the recommended replacement fluid (Cochrane: equivalent efficacy to albumin/plasma, lower cost, no infection risk, no NEC association).

Neonatal thrombocytopenia: plt < 150K/µL. Affects up to 25% of NICU admissions. Severity: mild 100–149K, moderate 50–99K, severe < 50K.

Neonatal platelets are hyporesponsive in vitro but have adequate hemostasis in vivo (higher VWF, larger VWF multimers). Neonates tolerate lower plt counts before clinical bleeding.

  2. Contact blood bank for HPA-1a-neg plts. If unavailable (24–48h), transfuse random donor plts as bridge.

~2% of Caucasians are HPA-1a negative. When HPA-1a-neg mother carries HPA-1a-pos fetus, ~10% chance of sensitization; ~30% of sensitized have affected infant.

• Recurrence: 80–90% if father homozygous; 50% if heterozygous
  • Severity equal or WORSE in subsequent pregnancies
  • Prenatal: maternal IVIG ± steroids from 20–28 wk; serial monitoring; planned delivery 36–37 wk; HPA-1a-neg plts at delivery
  • Paternal HPA genotyping guides risk
  • MFM + hematology referral for planning

• Most common cause (~75% of early cases)
  • Mechanism: reduced placental thrombopoietin + ↓ megakaryocyte production
  • Typical nadir: 50–100K; rarely <50K
  • Spontaneous recovery by day 7–10
  • Transfusion rarely needed (plts usually stay >25K)

• Daily plt count until trending up (usually day 5–7)
  • If drops <50K unexpectedly → reconsider diagnosis (NAIT? Infection?)
  • If drops <25K stable → transfuse per PlaNet-2
  • Full recovery: plt normalizes day 10–14

• Bacterial sepsis: #1 cause. Both Gram-pos and Gram-neg. Consumption + marrow suppression + DIC.
  • NEC: Falling plts may PRECEDE clinical NEC by 24–48h.
  • Fungal: Candida. Prolonged Abx + central lines + TPN + extreme prematurity.
  • DIC: ↑PT + ↑aPTT + ↓fib + ↑D-dimer.
  • Drug-induced: Heparin (HIT rare), indomethacin, vancomycin.

1. Blood culture (peripheral ± central line)
  2. CBC with diff — I:T ratio, ANC
  3. CRP and/or procalcitonin (PCT rises earlier: 2–4h vs CRP 6–12h)
  4. UA + UCx (catheterized)
  5. CSF if warranted and infant stable
  6. DIC panel: PT, aPTT, fibrinogen, D-dimer
  7. Start empiric Abx: vancomycin + aminoglycoside (or pip-tazo/meropenem per local antibiogram)
  8. Consider empiric antifungal if risk factors present

⚠️ Falling plts + abdominal distension + metabolic acidosis in preterm = NEC until proven otherwise. Stat abdominal radiograph. NPO, OG to suction, IV antibiotics.

Bell Stage II+ NEC is almost always accompanied by thrombocytopenia. Platelet trajectory can guide clinical decision-making: a suddenly dropping plt count is an early warning sign.

✓ IM vitamin K1 0.5–1 mg within 6 hours of birth for ALL newborns. Single injection prevents all three forms. AAP does NOT recommend oral vitamin K.

When parents refuse:

  • Counsel clearly: late VKDB = 50% ICH, 20% mortality
  • If still refuse IM: offer oral (2 mg PO at birth, 1 wk, 4 wk) — LESS effective
  • Document discussion and refusal
  • Flag chart for close follow-up

DIC paradox: Simultaneous THROMBOSIS (microthrombi → organ ischemia) AND HEMORRHAGE (factor/plt depletion → diffuse bleeding).

Triggers: Sepsis (#1), perinatal asphyxia/HIE, NEC, severe hemolytic disease, Kasabach-Merritt, hypothermia, MAS/PPHN.

🚨 DIC is NEVER a primary diagnosis. Always identify and treat the trigger. Factor replacement without treating the cause is futile.

1. #1 TREAT THE CAUSE: Sepsis → Abx. NEC → NPO/Abx/surgery. Asphyxia → supportive/TH.
  2. Replace factors: FFP 10–15 mL/kg. Cryo 5–10 mL/kg (fib <100). Plts 10–15 mL/kg.
  3. Maintain perfusion: Volume, inotropes, adequate ventilation.
  4. Monitor q4–6h: PT, aPTT, fib, plts, D-dimer.
  5. Heparin: Generally NOT used in neonatal DIC. Exception: purpura fulminans (protein C/S deficiency).

Hemophilia A (factor VIII def): X-linked; 1/5,000 males. Presents with circumcision/heel stick bleeding. Isolated ↑aPTT, normal PT. Severe <1%, moderate 1–5%, mild 5–40%. Treat: factor VIII concentrate 50 U/kg.

Hemophilia B (factor IX def): X-linked; 1/25,000. Clinically identical to A. Factor IX is vit K-dependent and normally low in neonates — confirm diagnosis at 3–6 months.

⚠️ Factor VIII reaches adult levels by 6 months gestation → hemophilia A CAN be diagnosed at birth. Factor IX is low normally → hemophilia B diagnosis unreliable until 3–6 months.

• Normal PT AND aPTT — NOT measured by standard screening tests
  • Classic: delayed umbilical stump bleeding (day 7–10)
  • ICH in 30%
  • Diagnosis: factor XIII activity level
  • Treatment: factor XIII concentrate; prophylaxis q4–6 weeks
🔬 All screening tests normal + bleeding = think factor XIII. The one factor NOT measured by PT or aPTT.

• Liver synthesizes virtually all clotting factors except VIII and VWF
  • Causes: neonatal hemochromatosis, herpes hepatitis, metabolic (galactosemia, tyrosinemia), biliary atresia, hepatic ischemia
  • Pattern: BOTH PT and aPTT prolonged + low albumin + elevated direct bili + elevated transaminases
  • Distinguished from DIC by less prominent D-dimer/schistocytes (unless concurrent DIC)
  • Management: vitamin K 1 mg IV, FFP for active bleeding, treat underlying liver disease

node.description: Sepsis vs maternal HTN vs alloimmune

content.html:
1. SICK? → Presume sepsis. Blood cx + empiric Abx immediately.
  2. WELL preterm + maternal preeclampsia/HTN? → Placental insufficiency. Monitor ANC daily. Resolves 3–5 days.
  3. WELL term + isolated neutropenia? → Consider alloimmune (maternal anti-neutrophil Ab). Self-limited.
  4. Persistent >2 wk or ANC <200? → Congenital (Kostmann, cyclic, Shwachman-Diamond). Hematology referral.

• G-CSF did NOT consistently reduce mortality in sepsis-associated neutropenia (Cochrane review)
  • NOT routinely recommended for sepsis
  • IS indicated for congenital neutropenia (chronic ANC <200)
  • Dose: 5–10 µg/kg/day SC or IV

• Elevated WBC alone does NOT diagnose infection
  • I:T >0.2: sensitive (~80%) but poor specificity (~30%); many false positives
  • Combine with clinical assessment + CRP/PCT + blood culture
  • WBC >50K with blasts → leukemoid reaction vs TAM (T21) vs congenital leukemia → urgent smear/hematology

Common benign causes:

  • Physiologic leukocytosis of birth (peaks 12–24h)
  • Maternal betamethasone/dexamethasone (24–48h effect)
  • Crying, stress, cold exposure (demargination)
  • Post-seizure (transient)

When NOT to treat: Well-appearing, afebrile neonate with elevated WBC at 12–24h, no risk factors, normal CRP → observe, do NOT start antibiotics based on WBC alone.
